pages.scope: US edition of the Canadian /blog/no-see-ums-biting-midges-ontario (regional pair), for the US head search "no see ums" (page one in the WebSearch screens is spam, pest and screen companies, repellent brands, A-Z Animals and news stories, with no extension page). The insect, not the bites (/blog/no-see-um-bites keeps those): what no-see-ums are (biting midges, Culicoides, family Ceratopogonidae; adults about 1 to 2 mm, under 1/16 inch; only females bite: UF/IFAS EENY-349 IN626), the names (no-see-ums, punkies, sand flies, sand gnats: one line), how to tell them from gnats, mosquitoes and black flies (a quick-ID table), where they live in the US (salt marshes and coasts of the Atlantic and Gulf, Florida, lakes and streams inland, the Southwest: UF/IFAS, University of Arizona), season and time of day (in Florida adults are most active June through August: UF/IFAS; dawn and dusk only as a source says), can they get indoors (standard window screens do not stop them; the mesh that does only as a source gives it), keeping them away (fans, fine mesh, repellents only as CDC or EPA list them, permethrin-treated clothing only as EPA says; why yard spraying does little: sources' strength), disease (no-see-ums and Oropouche or livestock bluetongue only at CDC or UF/IFAS strength; no US risk claim the sources do not make), and a two-sentence bite summary with at most one bite figure. pages.h1Hint: Cellar Spiders (Daddy Long Legs): Do They Bite, and How to Tell a Harvestman
pages.metaTitleHint: Cellar Spider (Daddy Long Legs): Bite and ID
pages.scope: Cellar spiders (family Pholcidae) for US and Canadian readers: the spider most people mean by "daddy long legs" indoors, identification and the bite question first. The quick answer: a tiny pale body on very long, thin legs, hanging upside down in a loose web in a basement, crawl space, garage or ceiling corner, that vibrates in its web until it blurs when disturbed, and that is not known to bite people (Penn State; UMN). Sizes only from sources (Penn State's long-bodied cellar spider: body about 1/4 to 5/16 inch, a female's front legs about 2 inches). The species people meet, each only as a source covers it: the long-bodied cellar spider, the most common of its family in the US (Penn State), the marbled cellar spider, which has displaced it in California (UC IPM), and the short-bodied cellar spider. "Cellar spider bite" and "are daddy long legs poisonous" answered at the sources' strength: Penn State says cellar spiders are not known to bite people; the story that they are the most venomous spider but cannot bite has no scientific basis, and harvestmen have no venom glands or fangs (UC Riverside's daddy-long-legs page; Missouri Dept. of Conservation); never a bite photo, never a diagnosis (bites in general: /blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like). "Cellar spider vs harvestman" gets its own h2 and the quick-ID table (traits as rows: body parts, eyes, silk and web, legs, where you find it, venom), from the sources: a harvestman has one oval body with no waist, two eyes and no silk (MDC), a cellar spider two body parts, a cluster of eyes and a messy web (Penn State, MDC). The third "daddy longlegs", the crane fly, gets one card and one line that link /blog/mosquito-hawk-explained, which keeps every crane fly search. Then the female carrying her eggs in her jaws (one line; /blog/spider-egg-sacs), what cellar spiders eat (only as a source says; answer "do daddy long legs eat silverfish" only if one does), why they live indoors all year, and what to do: leave them, or remove webs with a broom or vacuum (UMN); control goes to /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-spiders (planned) or /blog/house-spiders. Cards: harvestman, crane fly, common house spider (/blog/house-spiders), brown recluse ("cellar spider vs brown recluse" stays with /blog/brown-recluse-look-alikes: one line and a link), camel cricket (/blog/camel-crickets, the long-legged basement jumper called a spider cricket). Link /tools/spider-identifier as the next step. Sources: Penn State Extension (long-bodied cellar spider), UMN Extension, UC IPM, UC Riverside (Vetter), Missouri Dept. of Conservation, as already cited on /blog/house-spiders, /blog/venomous-spiders, /blog/spiders-in-california and /tools/spider-identifier. pages.h1Hint: Springtails: The Tiny Jumping Bugs in Bathrooms, Basements and Plant Soil
pages.metaTitleHint: Springtails: Tiny Jumping Bugs in the House
pages.scope: Springtails (Collembola) for US readers who find tiny jumping bugs indoors, identification first. The quick answer: tiny (sizes only from sources, inches first), soft-bodied and wingless, white, gray, black or banded, and they flip into the air with a forked, tail-like spring folded under the body; they need moisture and are a sign of it, and they do not bite people or damage the house (Colorado State, UMN, Penn State, UC IPM, whichever say so). The two body shapes people see (long-bodied and round, globular springtails) with photos at a printed scale. Where they turn up and why: tubs, sinks and shower drains, damp basements and window sills, wet potting soil after watering, pool water, and outdoors in mulch and leaf litter, sometimes in large numbers by foundations (each only as a source says); snow fleas, the springtails that dot late-winter snow, in one short section (a winter search). "Baby springtails": young springtails look like small adults (no larval stage), only as a source says. "Springtail or flea?" in one short section that links /blog/bugs-that-look-like-fleas, which keeps "springtails vs fleas"; the tiny-black-bug and houseplant searches stay with /blog/tiny-black-bugs and /blog/houseplant-bugs (link both). How to get rid of springtails, moisture first, in order: fix leaks and drips, ventilate the bathroom, run a dehumidifier, let houseplant soil dry between waterings, pull mulch and leaf litter back from the foundation, seal gaps, vacuum the ones indoors (Colorado State, UMN); insecticides only at the sources' strength (Colorado State advises avoiding them indoors where possible; UMN says there are no pesticides for springtails in houseplants), never a home-remedy spray. Quick-ID table: the springtail and its look-alikes (flea, booklouse, mite, fungus gnat larva in soil), one row each: size, color, how it moves, where you find it, bites or not. Cards: flea (/blog/bugs-that-look-like-fleas), booklouse (no link: /blog/booklice is slated for replacement), silverfish (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-silverfish), fungus gnat (/learn/how-to-get-rid-of-fungus-gnats). No product advice beyond the one generic pick; no quote prompt (a traffic page).

pages.scope: The flea dirt page, identification first: what flea dirt is (the digested blood adult fleas excrete as they feed: Ohio State, Texas A&M, the University of Florida's cat flea profile, Penn State's cat flea fact sheet), what it looks like at life size and magnified (black to reddish-black specks like ground pepper, comma-shaped up close: the University of Minnesota's veterinary diagnostics textbook, the Merck Veterinary Manual; a size only if a source gives one), and the wet paper towel test as the centerpiece, step by step: comb the pet over white paper, a white sink or a pillowcase, put the specks on a damp white paper towel, and flea dirt dissolves into reddish-brown smears where ordinary dirt does not (Ohio State, Minnesota, Merck, Cornell Feline Health Center). Where to look: on a dog, the neck, shoulder blades and base of the tail, belly and groin (Ohio State, Minnesota, Merck); on a cat, the back of the neck, the top of the tail head, belly and back (Cornell Feline Health Center); with a fine-toothed flea comb; then pet bedding, resting spots, beds and carpet, and for cats shelves and tabletops (Ohio State). A photo strip and quick-ID table, flea dirt vs ordinary dirt vs flea eggs vs dandruff, and look-alike cards (flea eggs; bed bug poop, which also runs red but stains mattress seams; cockroach specks). What finding it means: adult fleas are feeding on the animal now, even when none is seen (Merck: dogs very allergic to flea saliva may be almost free of fleas because they groom so much), and larvae develop where flea dirt collects because they feed on it (only as UF, UC IPM and Penn State put it); flea dirt but no fleas; flea dirt in a bed. Whether it is harmful, at the sources' strength: CDC's flea-borne typhus page (infected flea dirt rubbed into bites or other wounds; murine-typhus once live) and cat-scratch disease page (scratches contaminated with flea feces), anemia in heavily infested kittens and puppies (Cornell, Merck), tapeworm (Texas A&M, Cornell). What to do: treat every pet with a product a veterinarian recommends, never a dog product on a cat (Cornell; CDC: never permethrin on cats), wash pet bedding hot and vacuum often (UC IPM), then /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-fleas for the full plan; no product advice here. pages.metaTitleHint: Camel Cricket (Spider Cricket): ID and Control
pages.scope: Camel crickets for US and Canadian readers, identification first: a humpbacked, wingless cricket, light tan to dark brown, with antennae much longer than its body and large hind legs, that never chirps (no sound-making organs, per Clemson HGIC; chirping indoors points to field crickets, per NC State) and jumps a surprisingly long way (MDC); sizes only from sources (Clemson: 1/2 to 1 1/2 inches; MDC: body up to about 1 inch). The "jumps at you" reputation only as a source puts it: NC State, Clemson and MDC do not say they jump toward people, and it is never an attack. Which ones get into homes: the greenhouse camel cricket (Tachycines asynamorus, also written Diestrammena asynamora), the most common camel cricket in eastern US homes (Epps et al. 2014, PeerJ; NC State), and the native camel or cave crickets (Ceuthophilus); nymphs look like small adults (NC State). Then the "spider cricket" question, spider or cricket (six legs and long antennae against a spider's eight legs and none), with look-alike cards: house and field cricket (crickets-in-house, once live), cellar spider (/blog/house-spiders), wolf spider (/blog/wolf-spiders), house centipede (/blog/house-centipedes). Where they live and why they come in: damp basements, crawl spaces, garages and laundry rooms; outdoors under stones, logs, firewood, mulch and ivy; large numbers point to a moisture problem (MDC); whether they breed indoors, where sources differ (MDC and Iowa State: unlikely unless it stays dark and damp; Cornell's Nassau County office: they can). Bites and harm at the sources' strength: none of the sources read reports a bite (MDC and Kentucky call them harmless); damage only as Clemson (fine fabrics and houseplants when numerous) and NC State (stored garments and linens after a long infestation; dark fecal smears on joists) put it. A control section, since this page owns "how to get rid of camel crickets": dry the space, seal and weather-strip, pull mulch, firewood and stored boxes back from walls, sticky traps in corners and behind appliances, vacuum (NC State, Clemson); insecticides only as those sources put them (perimeter first, baits in crawl spaces, a product labeled for the site; the label is the law), no product names. One line each, linked once live: chirping crickets (crickets-in-house) and the unrelated desert camel spider (camel-spiders); the western Jerusalem cricket is another family (UC IPM), one line at most. Sources: NC State Extension's Camel Crickets (revised 2023), Clemson HGIC, University of Maryland Extension, University of Kentucky, MDC, Iowa State, Epps et al. 2014.

pages.scope: For US travelers, the hotel check first, in the order to do it. Keep luggage off the floor and off the bed until the check is done, on a luggage rack, table or other hard surface (University of Kentucky ENTFACT-636; EPA's Protecting Your Home from Bed Bugs says to inspect the luggage rack). Check the bed from the pillow end with a flashlight: sheets and pillows back, mattress seams, piping and tags, and the box spring where it can be seen (Kentucky); the headboard edges and the gap behind it, a frequent hiding place in hotel rooms, without taking it down (Kentucky warns untrained people not to); then the nightstand, upholstered chairs and the luggage rack straps. What the signs look like in a hotel bed (live bugs, ink-dot fecal spots, shed skins, eggs), with photos at life size, linking /blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist, /blog/bed-bug-poop and /blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like; why a clean check is not proof (Virginia Tech: in a new infestation, a hotel room for example, evidence can be very hard to find). If you find them: tell the front desk, ask for a room in a different part of the hotel because infestations sometimes extend to nearby units (Kentucky), photograph the evidence and keep luggage closed; who must act is set by states and cities, not EPA (EPA's Bed Bug Laws and Regulations page: 21 states with some law or regulation, focused mostly on hotels and landlords), stated at that strength, no legal advice. Bites during or after a trip: marks can take as long as 14 days to show and bites alone do not confirm bed bugs (CDC), and bites noticed after getting home do not mean the home is infested (Virginia Tech); link /blog/bed-bug-bites and /blog/bed-bug-bites-but-no-bed-bugs. Coming home: unpack away from the bedroom, put clothing straight into the washer or dryer (heat settings only as a source gives them), heat-treat or isolate a suitcase you are worried about (Kentucky: a hot car in summer; Rutgers: a portable heating box), why Kentucky rates inspecting or vacuuming a suitcase as less useful, how to watch for bed bugs at home afterwards (interceptors under the bed legs; /blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist) and what to do if they came home (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs). For perspective, Kentucky says most hotel infestations are limited to a few rooms. A where-to-check table (spot, what to look for, how to check it) and look-alike cards (bat bug, carpet beetle larva, cockroach nymph, spider beetle; /blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs). Hiding places in general go to /blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide. Sources: EPA (How to Find Bed Bugs; Protecting Your Home from Bed Bugs; Bed Bug Laws and Regulations), CDC, University of Kentucky ENTFACT-636, Virginia Tech, Rutgers and the Indiana Department of Health, as already cited on /blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide and /learn/bed-bugs. pages.scope: Bugs-in-a-place sorter (WRITER_BRIEF_PHOTO_ID format 2; models /blog/bugs-in-kitchen and /blog/bugs-in-bathroom) for the basement. Quick answer: most basement bugs are moisture lovers (house centipedes, camel crickets, silverfish, springtails, millipedes, pill bugs and sow bugs, cellar spiders), and drying the basement works on all of them (EPA's 30 to 50 percent indoor humidity target; extension sources). h2s by where and how the reader sees them: running across the floor or up a wall at night (house centipedes; camel crickets that jump; ground beetles; oriental cockroaches near floor drains); along walls and floor edges after rain (millipedes, pill bugs and sow bugs, earwigs: they come in from outside); tiny jumping or flying specks around a floor drain, sump pit or damp concrete (springtails, drain flies, fungus gnats from stored potting soil); in boxes, books and paper (silverfish and booklice; spider beetles in old stored food or nests); in corners and ceiling joists (cellar spiders, house spiders, the woodlouse spider); in winter, the overwintering invaders that end up in basements (link /blog/bugs-in-house-in-winter). Where they come from (moisture, cracks and gaps, window wells, mulch and leaf litter against the foundation) and the fix per bug from extension sources: dehumidify, fix leaks, gutters and grading, seal gaps and window wells, store boxes off the floor in sealed bins; no pesticide products (link each bug's own page). A how-to-tell checklist for the bug in a jar and a quick-ID facts table under the quick answer (size, color, where in the basement, crawls, jumps or flies, the one tell). Leave to other pages: camel crickets in basement (/blog/camel-crickets), centipedes in basement (/blog/house-centipedes), cellar spiders (/blog/daddy-long-legs), silverfish (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-silverfish), the dehumidifier searches. pages.scope: Answer page for "dust mite bites" (health publishers hold page one: aim for page one, not the top 3). The reader has itchy red bumps or a rash, often noticed in bed or on waking, and thinks dust mites are biting. Lead with a photo and the answer: dust mites do not bite people (they eat shed skin flakes); what they can do is trigger an allergy, and in some people that allergy shows on the skin, for example as itching or an eczema flare (only at NIH, NIEHS, MedlinePlus, AAD, a medical school or the Merck Manual's strength; never diagnose). Then: how an allergy flare differs from bites (only as the medical sources describe it); a "what is really biting you" table at the medical and extension sources' strength: bed bugs (bites on skin exposed in bed, often in rows or clusters: link /blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist, what-do-bed-bug-bites-look-like when live), fleas (ankles and lower legs: /blog/fleas-on-humans, flea-bites when live), bird and rodent mites (after a nest empties or rodents are removed: /blog/mite-bites), scabies (burrows, night itch, between the fingers: scabies-vs-bed-bugs when live), carpet beetle larvae (an itchy rash from their hairs: /blog/carpet-beetle-rash), chiggers and mosquitoes (bites picked up outdoors); how to check the bed for a real biter (link /blog/bed-bug-bites-but-no-bed-bugs); if dust mite allergy is the cause, a short summary of the NIEHS steps (encasements, hot-water washing, humidity), linking /blog/dust-mites for the detail; and a "When to get medical care" warning callout (a rash that spreads or does not improve, signs of infection, fever, wheezing or trouble breathing, suspected scabies: medical sources only). Quick-ID facts table under the quick answer (cause, what you see, where on the body, when, the tell). Medical rules (as on mite-bites): health claims only from CDC, NIH (NIEHS, MedlinePlus, NCBI Bookshelf), AAD, medical schools or the Merck Manual; mite biology may also come from a university extension; anti-itch care in general terms only, no product names or doses; allergy testing and treatment are a clinician's call. pages.h1Hint: Skunk Smell in the House: What Causes It, When It Could Be a Gas Leak and How to Get It Out
pages.metaTitleHint: Skunk Smell in the House? Causes and Fixes
pages.scope: Cause sorter for "skunk smell in house" (a thin, spam-filled page one: a cause checklist plus odor-removal steps should reach the top 3). The reader smells skunk inside, often at night, with no skunk in sight. Put the safety check first, in a warning callout: utilities add an odorant to natural gas so leaks can be smelled, and some people find it skunk-like; if it might be gas, leave now, do not use switches, phones or flames inside, and call 911 or the gas utility from outside (PHMSA's "Pipeline Leak Recognition and What to Do" or the utility's own wording, at their strength). Then the causes, each with its tell: a skunk sprayed near the house and the odor came in through windows, vents or an air intake; a skunk denning under a deck, porch, shed or crawl space (dens at ground level: University of Nebraska-Lincoln, ICWDM, a state wildlife agency); a pet that was sprayed; a dead skunk under the house (UNL: removing the carcass is what ends the odor; rabies caution); sewer gas from a dry drain trap (a university or state source); anything else only where a credible source names it. How to find the source (which rooms, when, after rain, after the pet came in). How to get the smell out at extension strength: ventilate; wash fabrics; the hydrogen peroxide, baking soda and dish soap mix for pets and people exactly as Penn State Extension ("Sprayed by a skunk") and UNL give it, mixed in an open container and used at once, never stored, kept out of eyes; what does not work only where a source says so. How to keep skunks out (seal openings under decks and porches only after making sure no animal or young is inside, one-way doors and timing outside the birthing season, as UNL and state agencies say; a summary linking /blog/raccoon-and-skunk-proofing-under-a-deck-canada); rabies: skunks are a rabies reservoir in the US (CDC); do not trap or handle them (UGA, as /blog/holes-in-yard says); a skunk acting sick or out by day goes to animal control or the state wildlife agency. Quick-ID facts table (cause, what you smell, where, when, what to do). Links: /blog/holes-in-yard (mustLink), /blog/animals-in-attic, /blog/animal-droppings, /blog/raccoon-and-skunk-proofing-under-a-deck-canada (neutral anchor). Not linked: amazon.ca product pages, service pages. No quote prompt, no wildlife-removal pitch.

pages.h1Hint: Wood Roaches: How to Tell a Wood Cockroach From the Roaches That Infest Homes (Photos)
pages.metaTitleHint: Wood Roach vs Cockroach: How to Tell (Photos)
pages.scope: Species page for "wood roach" (two thin university pages and brands on page one: page one is realistic, the top 3 needs links). The reader found a brown roach indoors, often in spring, near firewood or under a porch light, or a winged one that flew to a light, and wants to know whether it means an infestation. Quick answer: wood cockroaches (Parcoblatta, twelve North American species; the Pennsylvania wood cockroach is the most common) live outdoors under loose bark, in woodpiles and leaf litter; males have full wings and fly to lights; indoors they die within days and do not breed, so one is a nuisance, not an infestation, and pesticides are neither necessary nor recommended (Penn State Extension, University of Kentucky, Iowa State, University of Minnesota). Then: how to identify one (photos of male and female: males with long wings, females with short wings and a broad abdomen; pale edges on the wings and shield in some species; sizes up to about 1 inch; nymphs); wood roach vs German, American and Oriental cockroaches (a quick-ID facts table: size, color, wings, where found, breeds indoors or not; cards); why they come inside (lights at night, firewood brought in for winter, gaps around doors and windows: Kentucky, Penn State); when (at the sources' strength); are they harmful (not a known disease carrier, do not infest food or belongings: University of Minnesota); and what to do (exclusion: seal gaps and fit door sweeps, keep firewood outdoors and bring in only what you will burn, switch off or change outdoor lights; no sprays, as Penn State says). Leave to other pages: palmetto bugs and the Florida woods cockroach (/blog/palmetto-bugs), can cockroaches fly (/blog/can-cockroaches-fly), bugs that look like cockroaches (that page), baby cockroaches. Links: /learn/cockroaches and /blog/bugs-that-look-like-cockroaches (mustLink), /blog/can-cockroaches-fly, /blog/palmetto-bugs, /blog/where-do-cockroaches-come-from, /blog/german-cockroaches. pages.scope: Color sorter for "tiny red bugs" (WRITER_BRIEF_PHOTO_ID format 2, the tiny-black-bugs model). The reader sees tiny red specks or bugs on a wall, windowsill, patio, plant or their skin and wants to know what they are and whether they bite. Quick answer: indoors and on sunny walls in spring and fall the usual tiny red bug is the clover mite (smaller than a pinhead, red to reddish brown, very long front legs; harmless to people; leaves a red smear when crushed: University of Minnesota, Penn State, Maryland or South Dakota State Extension); outdoors the main biter is the chigger (larvae almost too small to see, called red bugs in the South); the rest are red velvet mites, spider mites on plants, boxelder bug nymphs on sunny walls, and red insects such as fire ants and velvet ants (each at an extension source's strength). h2s by where the reader sees them: on walls, windowsills and siding (clover mites, boxelder bug nymphs); on patios, sidewalks and soil (red velvet mites; clover mites on concrete); on plants (spider mites, red aphids: link /blog/spider-mites, /blog/houseplant-bugs); on your skin or after time outdoors (chiggers: you rarely see them, the bites show later, link /blog/chigger-bites and /blog/mite-bites; fire ants: /blog/red-ants; a red bug attached to the skin may be a tick: one line linking /blog/red-ticks-and-clover-mites); in bed (a bed bug nymph is bright red just after feeding: /blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like); in the pool (water mites, only if a source covers them); and which ones bite or sting (chiggers, fire ants, velvet ants, bed bugs) and which do not bite people (clover mites, red velvet mites, spider mites, boxelder bugs: sources). What to do about clover mites indoors (vacuum or wipe them up rather than crush them; seal gaps; a plant-free strip along the foundation: only as the extension source gives it; no miticide products). A size scale (pinhead, 1/32 inch, 1/8 inch) and a quick-ID facts table under the quick answer (bug, size, color, where, bites or not, the one tell).
